messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Arguments: Arguments, Uncertainty: Uncertainty
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 25-year-old married Vietnamese American woman who works as a database administrator for a mid-sized logistics company. When she speaks about the crash, she does so in fragments at first, then with sudden precision. It happened late in the evening as she and her husband were driving home after an argument that had stretched through dinner and followed them into the car. She had been tense, trying to decide whether to keep talking or let the silence sit, and she remembers the unstable feeling of not knowing what would happen next on the road or between them. At an intersection, another vehicle came fast into their path and the impact was violent enough that for a moment she was certain they were going to die. What has stayed with her most sharply is not only the force of the collision but the sense that events tipped beyond her control in a second while she was still caught up in what she should have said, whether she should have insisted on stopping, whether she should have done something different before the impact.

In the weeks afterward, Linh became fixed on the idea that the crash happened because of the way she acted. She went over the drive repeatedly, convinced that if she had spoken differently, insisted they pull over, or interrupted the argument sooner, the night would have gone another way. She says she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. Even when other people told her that a collision is not something one person can simply prevent by saying the right thing, she could not accept it. In her mind, there had been a narrow window when she might have changed everything, and failing to act in exactly the right way became proof to her of a serious personal failing.

Since the collision, ordinary moments have acquired a charged and dangerous quality. Arguments are especially difficult. If her husband raises his voice, even briefly, or if she hears coworkers snapping at one another across the office, she feels herself tense immediately. What unsettles her is not just the conflict itself but the conviction that arguments are the kind of moment in which disaster arrives. Uncertainty affects her in a similar way. An ambiguous text from her husband, a last-minute change in plans, or a confusing request at work can leave her feeling on edge, as though unpredictability means she is again seconds away from catastrophe. She describes being unable to tolerate not knowing, because not knowing feels too much like the moments before the crash.

Certain names also strike her with surprising force. Hearing names connected in her mind to the people involved, or names that sound close enough to pull her back to that night, can stop her in place. At work, where she spends long hours reviewing account records, server labels, and user tickets, this sometimes happens in the middle of a routine task. A name on an email chain or in a client record can make her stare at the screen and lose track of what she was doing. She has become more private about this at the office, worried that if people notice how easily shaken she is, they will see her as unreliable.

Over time, her life has narrowed. She avoids anything that puts her body under stress because the sensations frighten her. Climbing stairs too quickly, exerting herself, or doing anything that makes her heart pound feels intolerably close to the bodily alarm she remembers from the collision. She has stopped joining friends for outings and turns down invitations with excuses that sound practical but are mostly meant to keep her from being around other people. She has come to believe that people cannot be trusted, a belief that reaches beyond strangers to include friends whose reassurance feels shallow to her and coworkers whose intentions she now questions. Her husband has noticed that she pulls away from plans and conversations, and several friendships have thinned because she no longer answers messages or agrees to meet.

When thoughts of the crash crowd in too intensely, Linh sometimes hurts herself physically to stop thinking about it. She describes it not as wanting to die but as wanting, for a few moments, to force her mind onto something else. She is ashamed of this and has hidden it from nearly everyone, including her husband. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by how much energy went into staying ahead of arguments, uncertain situations, names that caught her off guard, and the physical sensations she no longer trusted in her own body. What finally brought her in was a recent argument at home followed by a day at work when a familiar-sounding name in a database ticket made her freeze at her desk and then spend the rest of the afternoon trying not to panic. She said she was frightened that her world was getting smaller and that she was becoming someone her husband and friends could no longer reach. At the same time, she still holds tightly to the fear that if she lets down her guard, fails to anticipate danger, or trusts too easily, something just as devastating could happen again.
